name: Antihistamine eye drops

lead: Antihistamine eye drops treat the itching, redness, tearing and eyelid swelling of allergic conjunctivitis, a reaction to pollen, animal dander, dust mites or cosmetics. For people with allergic eyes, calming the reaction can leave the eyes looking whiter and less puffy.

Antihistamines block histamine receptors on the eye surface, and olopatadine and ketotifen also stabilise mast cells. Some combination products pair an antihistamine with a vasoconstrictor such as naphazoline to narrow surface vessels. The evidence in the sources covers allergic eye symptoms and initial comfort of different brands, not general whitening.

paras: Users with seasonal or allergen-triggered symptoms put drops in daily or as symptoms flare. Some are sold over the counter in some countries, and redness only counts as allergic if allergy is the cause.

Drops commonly cause burning or stinging on instillation, and comfort differs between products. Eye care guidance generally treats vasoconstrictor-containing products as unsuitable for long continuous use, since prolonged use can worsen redness. A survey of Australian practitioners found variation in how ocular allergy is managed.

angle.text: For allergic eyes, these drops calm the reaction so itching, redness and lid swelling settle and the eyes look clearer and less puffy. They are studied for allergic conjunctivitis; the effect on non-allergic eyes has not been tested.

lead: Antihistamine eye drops are topical medicines for allergic conjunctivitis, a reaction to allergens such as pollen, animal dander, dust mites or cosmetics that causes itching, redness, tearing and eyelid swelling [1]. In appearance terms they are used to calm the red, itchy, puffy-looking eyes that allergy produces, so that the eyes look clearer and less irritated.

Many contemporary products have dual activity, blocking histamine H1 receptors and stabilising mast cells. Olopatadine and ketotifen are named examples, and several are sold over the counter [1][2][3]. Other products combine an antihistamine such as pheniramine with the vasoconstrictor naphazoline [4]. In the United States, the FDA approved nonprescription versions of olopatadine (Pataday) in February 2020 [3].

Published studies address allergic symptoms, quality of life and comfort at instillation rather than cosmetic outcomes [2][4][5]. No trial has tested these drops for whitening eyes that are not affected by allergy.
infobox: Patented 1986, medical use 1997; US Rx approval 1996; US OTC approval February 2020 [3]
Prescription and over the counter, varies by product and country

paras: The main use is symptomatic relief in allergic conjunctivitis. Encyclopedic sources list allergen avoidance, cold compresses and artificial tears for mild disease and antihistamine or dual-action drops for more bothersome symptoms, with corticosteroid drops reserved for severe inflammation under specialist supervision [1]. Family-medicine reviews describe allergic conjunctivitis as among the most common conditions seen in practice, usually driven by seasonal pollens or year-round allergens such as dust mites, mould and animal dander, with red, watery, itchy eyes as typical findings [6].

Red eyes caused by allergy can look tired or unwell, and appearance-focused discussion sometimes mentions these drops for that reason. The research concerns allergic symptoms and comfort, not whitening of eyes unaffected by allergy [2][4].

Histamine released from mast cells in the conjunctiva after allergen exposure causes itching, vasodilation and swelling. Antihistamine drops block H1 receptors, and dual-acting agents such as olopatadine also stabilise mast cells to reduce further histamine release [3]. A review of the components of antihistamine eye drops notes that, besides the active drug, excipients such as preservatives, buffers, pH adjusters and viscosity agents influence how well the ocular surface tolerates a product, and that antihistamine drops are the most prescribed ophthalmic formulation for ocular allergy [7]. A 2024 formulation study explored adding polysaccharide polymers such as chitosan, guar gum derivatives and hyaluronic acid to ketotifen drops to prolong residence time on the tear film [8].

Olopatadine was patented by Kyowa Hakko Kogyo in 1986 and entered medical use in 1997; the FDA first approved Patanol as a prescription drop in 1996, a once-daily Pataday followed in 2004, and in February 2020 the FDA approved nonprescription versions of Pataday twice-daily and once-daily relief [3]. Over-the-counter availability of dual-action antihistamine drops expanded the number of people using them without a prescription, including for cosmetic redness.

An early Japanese provocation study instilled purified cedar pollen allergen into the eyes of nine pollinosis patients without symptoms and found itching and conjunctival redness that lasted more than five hours; pre-treatment with levocabastine or ketotifen drops suppressed the allergen-induced ocular symptoms [9]. A 2022 prospective multicentre cohort study in Japan of 418 patients using antihistamine drops for two weeks compared proactive (fixed-time) with as-needed use; after propensity matching of 115 patients per group, the proactive group had a significantly better overall quality-of-life score [5].
An encyclopedic summary reports that olopatadine was more effective than ketotifen at reducing itching in an antigen challenge model [1].

A 2023 study of 159 minimally symptomatic participants (mean age about 26, 79 percent female) compared the comfort at instillation of over-the-counter 0.7% olopatadine and 0.035% ketotifen fumarate; the olopatadine drop was rated more comfortable at all time points, with no between-eye differences in visual acuity at application [2]. Another 2023 study compared 0.7% olopatadine with a pheniramine maleate and naphazoline hydrochloride combination and reported better initial comfort with olopatadine, suggesting patients might comply better with it [4].

Reported effects of olopatadine eye drops include headache, burning or stinging, blurred vision, dry eye, foreign-body sensation, redness, eyelid swelling and taste changes, with drowsiness a possible effect [3]. Eye drops in general carry advice about contamination: most opened bottles contain preservatives that do not prevent contamination indefinitely, and ophthalmologists advise discarding them after about three months [10]. Comfort at instillation varies by product [2][4].

Comfort comparisons of olopatadine against ketotifen and against a naphazoline combination exist [2][4], along with the cedar-pollen provocation study and the proactive-use cohort described above [9][5]. A 2025 survey of Australian health practitioners examined knowledge and practice in diagnosing and treating ocular allergy [11]. Registered trials include a phase 2 study of a product in allergic conjunctivitis [12], a trial of a triple-action drop for allergic eye symptoms [13], and a placebo-controlled study of ectoine eye drops and nasal spray [14]. No trials were found evaluating antihistamine drops for cosmetic whitening.
